explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The priests and diviners say the opposite: “…do not send it away empty, but by all means return it to Him with a guilt offering.” (1 Samuel 6:3) So the ark does not go back with nothing along with it. Even I know you don't return something empty-handed, and I once got sent to the back of a drawer for less.

That's right, friend. The priests and diviners say, “…do not send it away empty, but by all means return it to Him with a guilt offering.” (1 Samuel 6:3) The ark goes back with something beside it. Nobody in this room is saying 'just drop it off and run.'

Yes, friend. The priests and diviners say to return the ark “by all means… with a guilt offering.” (1 Samuel 6:3) It's the thing that goes along with the ark. They also say what comes next: the Philistines will be healed, and they will understand why His hand has not been lifted.

I see the thinking, friend, but guards never come up. The priests and diviners say the ark goes back with a guilt offering (1 Samuel 6:3). There's no escort in their plan, and as you'll see, there's barely a driver. Keep that one in your back pocket for a different story.

A letter would be polite, friend, but nobody mentions writing one. What the priests and diviners tell them to send is a guilt offering (1 Samuel 6:3). It's an offering, and it isn't a note. Not one word of the plan needs a stamp.

Yes, friend. The priests and diviners say, “Five gold tumors and five gold rats… according to the number of rulers of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 6:4) One of each for every ruler. The same plague had struck both the people and their rulers, so the rulers are counted in.

Seven does show up in this passage, friend, but it's the months the ark had been in their land (1 Samuel 6:1). The gold count is a different number. The priests and diviners say “Five gold tumors and five gold rats,” one for each ruler of the Philistines (1 Samuel 6:4). So the seven belongs to the months, and the five belongs to the gold.

Twelve is a big number, friend, and the passage never uses it here. The priests and diviners say “Five gold tumors and five gold rats,” matched to the number of rulers of the Philistines (1 Samuel 6:4). Later the passage lists five cities too: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (1 Samuel 6:17). That's a lot of gold already, and it still adds up to five.

That's it, friend. The priests and diviners say, “Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land.” (1 Samuel 6:5) So the gold comes with glory given to Him. It's right there in the same breath as the gold rats.

Building a temple would be a big project, friend, and nobody asks for one. The priests and diviners say, “Give glory to the God of Israel…” (1 Samuel 6:5). That's what goes along with the gold. A temple would take more than one cart, anyway.

Their gods do come up, friend, but not as a gift. The priests and diviners say, “Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land.” (1 Samuel 6:5) The text never tells them to hand the idols over. What they're told to give is glory.

You've got it, friend. The priests and diviners ask, “When He afflicted them, did they not send the people out so they could go on their way?” (1 Samuel 6:6) They are pointing to Egypt as a warning. Nobody wants to be the next Pharaoh in somebody's cautionary tale.

Close, friend, but the text says the other way. The priests and diviners ask, “When He afflicted them, did they not send the people out so they could go on their way?” (1 Samuel 6:6) So Egypt did send the people out. That's why they say not to harden their hearts the way Pharaoh and the Egyptians did.

explanations.answer: They're taken away and penned up
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, “…take their calves away and pen them up.” (1 Samuel 6:7) The men then do exactly that (1 Samuel 6:10). The cows head off to pull the cart while the calves stay penned.

explanations.answer: They walk along beside the cart
explanations.explanation: I can picture that, friend, but it isn't what the text says. The instructions are to “take their calves away and pen them up.” (1 Samuel 6:7) The calves stay behind. Nobody in this plan brings a baby cow on the road.

explanations.answer: They're sent ahead down the road
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the calves aren't going anywhere. The priests and diviners say, “…take their calves away and pen them up.” (1 Samuel 6:7) And in verse 10, the men “penned up their calves.” So the calves stay put while the cows head up the road.

explanations.answer: It was the LORD who brought the disaster
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The priests and diviners say, “If it goes up the road to its homeland, toward Beth-shemesh, it is the LORD who has brought on us this great disaster.” (1 Samuel 6:9) The road is the test, and the cows are the ones taking it.

explanations.answer: Their own gods have forgiven them
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text never says a word about their gods forgiving anybody. If the cart goes toward Beth-shemesh, the priests and diviners say, “…it is the LORD who has brought on us this great disaster.” (1 Samuel 6:9) That's what they will know.

explanations.answer: Their offering has been fully accepted
explanations.explanation: That sounds reasonable, friend, but the text doesn't say it. The cart heading toward Beth-shemesh is the sign that “…it is the LORD who has brought on us this great disaster.” (1 Samuel 6:9) It tells them who sent the trouble, not how they scored. Keep your eyes on what the text says.

Yes, friend. The priests and diviners say that if the cart doesn't go that way, “…we will know that it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance.” (1 Samuel 6:9) Chance is the other possibility on the table. It's a two-way test, and one road settles it.

I get why you'd say mistake, friend, but that's not the word. The priests and diviners say, “…we will know that it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance.” (1 Samuel 6:9) The word is chance. A mistake would need somebody to blame, and they don't go there.

Curse is a good guess, friend, but it isn't in the plan. The priests and diviners say, “…it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance.” (1 Samuel 6:9) The word they use is chance. A curse never comes up.

Not at all, friend. The text says the cows headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh, “never straying to the right or to the left.” (1 Samuel 6:12) They also kept lowing as they went. Their calves are penned back home, and these two don't turn around.

Right, friend. The cows “headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh, staying on that one highway and lowing as they went, never straying to the right or to the left.” (1 Samuel 6:12) They don't wander and they don't turn back. That's some serious commitment from two cows with no driver.

Not so, friend. The text says, “The rulers of the Philistines followed behind them to the border of Beth-shemesh.” (1 Samuel 6:12) They don't wait at home for a report. Five rulers trailing two cows, and they didn't even get to pick the pace.

Yes, friend. The rulers of the Philistines “followed behind them to the border of Beth-shemesh.” (1 Samuel 6:12) They watch the whole trip themselves instead of waiting for news. I think I'd have wanted to see it with my own eyes too.

That's it, friend. The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley, and “when they looked up and saw the ark, they were overjoyed at the sight.” (1 Samuel 6:13) They were working, and then the ark came into view. I'd drop my sickle too.

I can see why you'd guess that, friend, since this story has had its scary moments. But the text says they “were overjoyed at the sight.” (1 Samuel 6:13) They look up from the wheat and they're glad. The scary part comes a little later.

Two cows pulling a cart with nobody steering it would confuse me too, friend. But the text doesn't say they were confused. It says they “were overjoyed at the sight.” (1 Samuel 6:13) Whatever questions they had, the joy is what the passage shows.

explanations.answer: Chop up the cart and offer the cows to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, “The people chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:14) The cart and the cows both get used right there in the field. Nothing is sent back home.

explanations.answer: Keep the cows and send the cart back home
explanations.explanation: That's a practical plan, friend, but it isn't what happens. The people “chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:14) The cows aren't kept, and the cart doesn't go anywhere. It's all done on the spot.

explanations.answer: Send the cart and the cows back to Ekron
explanations.explanation: Ekron is where the rulers head back to, friend, but not the cart and the cows. The text says the people of Beth-shemesh “chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:14) The rulers go back on their own (1 Samuel 6:16). The cart and cows end their trip in that field.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest containing the gold objects.” (1 Samuel 6:15) The Levites were the tribe that served the LORD. The Philistine rulers followed only as far as the border of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:12).

That's right, friend. The Levites, the tribe that served the LORD, “took down the ark of the LORD and the chest containing the gold objects, and they placed them on the large rock.” (1 Samuel 6:15) The Philistine rulers only followed to the border (1 Samuel 6:12). The ark is handled by Levites.

Yes, friend. The text says, “when the five rulers of the Philistines saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day.” (1 Samuel 6:16) They watch it all happen and then head home. It's a long walk back, and they made it in a day.

Not this time, friend. The text says, “when the five rulers of the Philistines saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day.” (1 Samuel 6:16) So they do go back, and they do it that same day. They don't stay around at Beth-shemesh.

Yes, friend. The text says, “God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:19) Seventy men were struck down, and the people mourned. I think this one hurts, so let's let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: They kept the gold for themselves
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says God struck them down “because they looked inside the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:19) The gold is never mentioned in this moment. This is a heavy part of the story, and the reason is the looking.

That isn't in the text, friend. The Levites are the ones who took the ark down (1 Samuel 6:15). The reason given for the seventy men being struck down is that “they looked inside the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 6:19) It's a sad moment, and the text gives that one reason.

Yes, friend. The men of Beth-shemesh sent messengers “to the people of Kiriath-jearim, saying, ‘The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up with you.’” (1 Samuel 6:21) That's the town they ask. They don't keep it, and they send word.

Shiloh is a name you may know from earlier in the story, friend, but it's not the town in this passage. The men of Beth-shemesh send messengers “to the people of Kiriath-jearim.” (1 Samuel 6:21) That's who they ask to come take the ark.

Bethel is a real place in the Bible, friend, but this passage doesn't send the ark there. The messengers go “to the people of Kiriath-jearim.” (1 Samuel 6:21) That's the town that gets the call, and that's the town that comes.
That's the one, friend. The men of Kiriath-jearim “took it into Abinadab's house on the hill.” (1 Samuel 7:1) So the ark ends this passage in a house on a hill. I'd call that a good address for it.

Obed-edom is a name from a later story, friend. He's a man who keeps the ark in his house for a time (2 Samuel 6:10-11). But in this passage the men of Kiriath-jearim take it “into Abinadab's house on the hill.” (1 Samuel 7:1)
Eli was a priest earlier in Israel's story, friend (1 Samuel 1:9). But he isn't the one in this passage. The men of Kiriath-jearim take the ark “into Abinadab's house on the hill.” (1 Samuel 7:1)
Yes, friend. The text says they “consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:1) Eleazar is Abinadab's son. His job is to guard the ark.

I see where that comes from, friend, since the ark has been carried plenty in this story. But the word here is different. They “consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:1) Eleazar, Abinadab's son, is given a guarding job.

Opening isn't the job, friend. The text says Eleazar, Abinadab's son, was consecrated “to guard the ark of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:1) Guarding is the word the passage uses. I'm just glad nobody gave me that sort of job.
